idiom_name: opaque handle struct with paired create/destroy functions
implementation_notes: C has neither destructors nor ownership types, so the whole is an ordinary struct - usually exposed as an opaque handle - and the invariant lives in a create/destroy pair: X_create allocates and initialises the whole together with every part it owns, X_destroy releases the parts in reverse order and then the whole itself. The header must document who frees what (Fuchsia's C API guidelines ask for unambiguous ownership and an explicit create/take naming convention for transfers), and borrowed parts must never be released by the whole. Parts are embedded structs when the set is fixed or owned pointers when it grows; the classic Whole-Part structure remains the right form whenever a module owns several parts plus a shared invariant, while a plain value struct that the caller keeps on the stack is the smaller answer for pure data.
pitfalls: Nothing stops a caller from copying the struct by value, using the handle after destroy, or freeing a part directly: ownership must be documented per function and encoded in the types where possible (opaque handle, const pointers for borrowed parts).
Pointer parts add an allocation and a partial-construction path: create must free whatever it already allocated before returning an error, and destroy must tolerate a NULL handle.
Parts stored by value cannot grow while parts stored behind pointers lose the whole's locality - choose per part kind instead of uniformly.
